topics.title: 26.1 Missing pages
topics.summary: A missing translation can correspond to a legitimate region whose physical backing has not yet been installed. Anonymous memory can be provided lazily, and file-backed mappings can bring in pages as needed. Deferring work avoids allocating and reading pages that the application never touches. A missing page can also correspond to no valid mapping at all. The handler must consult the mapping policy rather than assume that any requested address deserves storage. Otherwise, invalid pointers would silently create new memory instead of being rejected.

topics.title: 26.2 Protection faults
topics.summary: A protection fault occurs when a mapping exists or is described, but the attempted operation is not permitted by the active protection state. Writing to a read-only mapping and fetching instructions from a non-executable mapping are examples under the relevant hardware configuration. Some protection faults are intentionally recoverable, notably copy-on-write. Others indicate an error. The handler must distinguish the region’s logical policy from its current hardware permission bits. A read-only code page is not made writable simply because a process attempted a store.

topics.title: 26.3 Demand paging
topics.summary: Demand paging supplies a page when it is actually needed. For a file mapping, the kernel can obtain the corresponding file data; for anonymous memory, it can provide zero-initialized storage consistent with the mapping’s semantics. Existing cached data can avoid a new storage-device read. The performance consequence depends on the work required. Some faults can be satisfied without reading from storage; others wait for I/O. A fault count without classification and workload context is therefore an incomplete performance metric. The same number of faults can represent very different elapsed costs.

topics.title: 26.4 Fault handling
topics.summary: Conceptually, handling involves identifying the faulting address and access, locating the mapping policy, validating the operation, obtaining suitable backing, updating translation structures, and resuming or rejecting the instruction. The kernel must synchronize this work with concurrent mapping changes and other faults. Application error handling usually does not attempt to repair arbitrary invalid pointer faults. Recovering from a corrupted execution state is much harder than catching a normal return-code error. Design programs to prevent invalid access and use operating-system errors for expected resource failures. Signal handling is discussed separately in Chapter 41.

topics.title: 26.5 Copy-on-write
topics.summary: Copy-on-write lets logically independent mappings share backing until a writer requires a private version. After fork , parent and child can initially share many physical pages while observing private-memory semantics. A write fault can cause the kernel to create a private copy for the writer and update its mapping. [ R15 ] A physical copy is not mandatory in every write-fault case. If the kernel determines that the backing is no longer shared in a way requiring separation, it may be able to make the page writable without copying. The semantic guarantee is private modification, not a promise that every store invokes a particular copying algorithm.

SLIDE 12: 26.5 Copy-on-write

LECTURE NARRATION
Copy-on-write lets logically independent mappings share backing until a writer requires a private version. After fork , parent and child can initially share many physical pages while observing private-memory semantics. A write fault can cause the kernel to create a private copy for the writer and update its mapping. [ R15 ] A physical copy is not mandatory in every write-fault case. If the kernel determines that the backing is no longer shared in a way requiring separation, it may be able to make the page writable without copying. The semantic guarantee is private modification, not a promise that every store invokes a particular copying algorithm.
